industry: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production
cause: Dropped objects
narrative:
An operator was removing a grating panel with manual handling hooks on the weather deck. 
During the operation, the grating unhooked from the manual handling tools and fell through the opening, hit a cable 
gate before landing on the underlying deck, approximately 10 meters below. The grating measures 1x1 meter and 
weighs 52,4 kg which gives a kinetic energy of 5149, 44 Joules. No one was injured, but under slightly changed 
circumstances people could have been in the line of fire as the deck was not cordoned off and there was a work 
team close to the area where it dropped.
what_went_wrong:
The grating was not physically secured.
During job preparation, the work crew had not reviewed all the required safety measures before starting the job, nor 
verified that they had been implemented, such as securing tools and equipment to prevent them from falling and 
barricading the area below the work site. No supervisor present to correct.
corrective_actions:
• When working at height, it is essential to ensure that tools and equipment are secured to prevent falling objects, 
in accordance with life-saving rules.
• When installing grating, it must always be secured with a fixed barrier, such as a shackle or wire/sling (the two-
barrier principle), as shown in the image to the right.
• Grating like this should be secured to the structure above the work area. The securing equipment should be as 
short as practically possible.
• The area below must always be sufficiently cordoned off.

narrative:
During the workboat transfer operation, workboat was transferred from the laydown area to the transport vessel 
main deck and positioned in its transport cradle. During final positioning, the vessel could not remain steady. As a 
result, the workboat swung into a nearby Cargo Carrying Unit (CCU), causing damage to the hull. A crew member 
handling a tag line was exposed to risk and was nearly caught between the CCU and the swinging workboat.
what_went_wrong:
• Clear Deck policy (no persons on deck during lifting operations) not adhered.
• Use of tag lines should have been properly assessed and if required, deviated against.
• Permit to work not used as per vessel Bridging document, for control of non routine tasks within safety zone.
• Methodology for transferring the workboat was not adequality assessed (MoC) rather a generic lifting risk 
assessment was used.
• Banksman did not have direct communication with vessel bridge, who were responsible for vessel positioning.
• Escape route for those involved in lifting route not clear, potential crushing scenario against container on deck, 
as work boat swung once lifted out of cradle.
corrective_actions:
• Provide an approved and certified cradle for workboats intended for lifting operations.
• Issue and reinforce a mandatory safety communication during safety meetings emphasizing the requirement for 
personnel involved in lifting operations to maintain a clear and unobstructed escape route.
• Review the competency levels of personnel involved in lifting operations and provide retraining where gaps are 
identified.
• Issue a formal communication requiring permit-to-work compliance and task-specific risk assessments for all 
non-routine activities within designated safety zones.
• Amend the company standard to formally include the prohibition of tag lines and the requirement to maintain a 
clear deck policy during boat lifting operations.

industry: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production
cause: Dropped objects
narrative:
A trailer driver was transporting six concrete barriers (3.5t each) on a flatbed trailer. The barriers were stacked in 
two rows (three in each row), with one cargo lashing belt securing two concrete barriers each. While the trailer was 
travelling on the bumpy road, the driver noticed that one of the lashing belts securing the rear concrete barriers 
had broken, causing the load to shift slightly towards the edge of the trailer. He pulled over to address the situation. 
Fortunately, no injuries or damage occurred.
what_went_wrong:
• The concrete barriers were loaded onto the truck without appropriate measures in place - no dunnage was used 
and there was inadequate load restraint.
• The driver used improvised lashing belts without proper inspection. One of these improvised belts broke during 
transportation on the bumpy road.
• The driver did not recognise the risk of using defective and improvised lashing belts.
corrective_actions:
• Always ensure all loads are properly loaded and restrained in accordance with appropriate lashing protocols to 
prevent them from shifting during transportation.
• Always use additional support systems like rubber mats and/or dunnage to increase the clamp down effect 
(friction between the load and the trailer surface) to prevent the load from shifting. 
• Always ensure loading crews and driver clearly understand the importance of the pre-trip Inspection – lashing 
belts and tools must be thoroughly inspected for wear, damage, and suitability before departure. Early detection 
of weakened or compromised equipment can prevent incidents. 
• Always ensure corrective actions are implemented at the earliest opportunity to prevent recurrence of similar 
incidents/accidents – there was a similar incident three months earlier.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
A chemical operator was performing a transfer and dosing operation of a caustic product into a cooling water 
system in an industrial plant. During the disconnection of a hose used for product injection (in an improvised 
location), residual pressure caused the chemical to splash onto the operator’s face and over his protective coverall. 
In reaction, the operator jumped from a portable ladder (about 1.5 meters high), resulting in a twisted ankle in 
addition to the chemical burn. The worker received immediate first aid and required medical attention, leading to 
time off work.
what_went_wrong:
What went wrong was that the task was performed using an improvised procedure, without any specific instructions 
or operational manuals covering the scenario. Deficiencies were evident in the management of operational 
changes, as there was no dedicated plan or risk analysis in place for the modified chemical injection point. The 
operator was using regular personal protective equipment, but did not have the specific goggles recommended 
for handling this chemical. Furthermore, communication regarding system changes and status was insufficient, 
resulting in misunderstandings about equipment availability and the associated risks. Maintenance backlogs forced 
the adoption of alternative and less safe methods, thus exposing workers to additional hazards. Additionally, there 
was a lack of structured practical training for new or less experienced operators, and critical tasks were carried out 
alone, without verification or support from a second trained person.
corrective_actions:
This event underscored the need for strong management of operational changes, effective communication, risk 
analysis, and continuous improvement of procedures and training to prevent recurrence of such incidents.
Key recommendations:
• Formalization of operational procedures for selected critical activities, including structured risk analysis.
• Reinforcement of internal communication to ensure any system changes are fully understood by all involved.
• Implementation of structured practical training for new operators, emphasizing human factors and safe 
execution.
• Creation of formal mechanisms that enable employees to report uncertainties and safely interrupt activities in 
case of doubt.
• Promotion of leadership workshops to reinforce the requirement for opening and managing changes for any 
operational deviations.

industry: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production
cause: Dropped objects
narrative:
When filling a mud tank with brine to prepare for cleaning of the tank, the transfer hose became dislodged, fell 
towards the ground (2.6m) and began to whip. The hose struck the pump operator’s leg, who suffered a ruptured 
Achilles tendon. The operator required surgery, classifying this as a Lost Work Day Case under IOGP guidelines. The 
incident is considered high potential, as the heavy hose coupling could have caused a fatality if it struck the head of 
the injured person when it fell.
what_went_wrong:
The original configuration of the activity was changed by the work team to run the lay-flat ‘fire’ hose into the top of 
the mud tank where there was no connection point. The pump was started without the hose being properly 
restrained and flow was too strong for the arrangements, causing the hose to dislodge and fall towards the injured 
person who was operating the pump at the base of the mud tank. 
Before the change in the configuration of the work, the job had been considered low risk. The change in risk 
introduced was not realised by the work team, who did not forecast potential movement of the hose.
corrective_actions:
Immediate actions:
1. Immediately issue / communicate a site instruction (or similar) requiring securing of hoses and hose ends
2. As an instruction, or an additional step in the risk assessment for the main tank cleaning job, state a preference 
to use a vacuum truck for filling, and if not available, acceptable alternative arrangements. Include hose type, 
suitable pump sizes, hose securing to tank utilizing fixed points, protection against failure of the system (e.g. whip 
checks) and position of people.
Preventative actions:
3. Committed to installing fixed hose connections to all tanks and chambers within the tanks to ensure hoses 
remain fixed and secure during pumping activities.
4. Implement dynamic risk assessment programme: Personnel will need to be trained on this simple process 
and when to conduct it (e.g. before each new task, a change, or a change in the mode of work or location). Such a 
process will provide a ‘pause’ before work, giving an opportunity to review risks and team actions, even for work that 
does not require a permit or formal risk assessment.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
An incident occurred during the transfer of an amine solution from a truck to a storage tank. The transfer 
was performed using a corrugated flexible hose connected to the truck with a threaded coupling and to the 
tank with a metal clamp. The end of the transfer was verified by observing hose vibrations generated during 
nitrogen displacement operations. After completing the transfer, one operator closed the nitrogen valve used for 
pressurization toward the truck and visually confirmed closure of the amine discharge valve on the truck. The 
second operator entered the containment area to close the tank valves. After closing the needle valve located near 
the tank, while attempting to close the ball valve, the hose suddenly detached from the nozzle, causing an amine 
splash that hit the operator’s face through a gap between the visor and the chin. While attempting to wash at the 
eyewash station, the operator rubbed his face and eyes with contaminated hands, worsening the injury. He was 
immediately assisted by a colleague, taken to the infirmary, and then transported to the emergency room.
what_went_wrong:
Design: the absence of a non-return valve in the tank isolation circuit was identified, although it was included in the 
reference P&ID. The NRV was designed to be installed between the two tank isolation valves. Its presence would 
have prevented the incident by avoiding amine backflow into the final section of the pipeline, caused by the tank 
head, during the operator’s movement from the truck to the tank to perform valve closure and tank isolation.
Management of Change: A MoC was underway to replace the current metal clamp fastening system used to connect 
the corrugated hose to the storage tank connections with safer fittings connections. The MoC process had started 
two years earlier. Engineering activities had been completed, and implementation had been finalized for some tanks 
but not yet for the tank involved in the incident.
Operational Procedure Misalignment: The existing loading procedure had been issued for a future plant 
configuration, as it was based on the implementation of the above-mentioned MoC, and therefore did not reflect the 
current operating conditions of the tank involved. Additionally, although the tank-side valve closing sequence was 
correctly performed by the operator, it did not include a clear and standardized sequence, generating confusion 
among operators due to the absence of a standard valve closure procedure.
Emergency Response Training: Insufficient awareness of decontamination procedures was identified. The eye injury 
occurred when the operator rubbed his eyes with contaminated hands.
corrective_actions:
Ensure technical/operational integrity: Verify that all design specifications are met during construction and 
installation. Address safety operational improvements deviations promptly through a completed MoC process and 
always ensure dedicated risk assessment which identifies possible mitigation measures to be implemented.
Keep procedures current: Operating procedures must reflect actual plant conditions, with clear roles, 
responsibilities, and standardized sequences
Strengthen emergency preparedness: Conduct regular training and drills for chemical exposure scenarios, 
including loading/unloading operations, to reinforce response protocols.

industry: Oil and Gas Production and Operations
narrative:
At 18:00 hrs on 11/30/2025, on-call personnel notified the Production Supervisor via radio about an event in the 
measurement tank (TM) area, detecting on site the passage of liquids in the suction valve from TM-1 to the RA-11 
oily register, which caused an increase in levels in the API dam and RA-05 oily registers (separator area), RA-12 
(measuring tank dam) and S/N registers in the area of pumps with hydrocarbon spillage on the ground of these 
areas, immediately an attempt was made to pump with the Internal Combustion Motor Pump 03 (MBCI-03) in a 
discontinuous manner due to the low suction pressure, so the suction valve of the TM-1 was dismantled. managing 
to contain the passage of liquid to the API dam and oily registers with diversion of oil to the TM containment dam 
and later pumping to the vertical tanks through the pump (MBCI-03).
what_went_wrong:
On the day of the event, Tank TM-1 had been dewatered by opening the suction valve towards its base, directing 
water to the API separator via the oily drains. During this operation the water was pumped from the API separator 
to the larger vertical storage tank TV-5. Once the water had been decanted the valve was closed.
Later in the afternoon an operator detected flow in the oily water system and determined that the valve on TM-1 was 
passing. Suspecting debris was lodged beneath the gate, the operator opened the valve to flush the debris and then 
closed it. This and other attempts to fully close the valve were unsuccessful and the operator decided to use a pipe 
wrench to close it. The force broke the lifting nut and there was a significant increase in flow.
Despite the pump running at the API separator and additional pumping of oil to the export system, the site was 
unable to prevent the API separator from being overwhelmed, and oil backflowed up the oil drainage system, 
overtopping covers in several locations to spill onto the concrete hardstanding. A flange was loosened at the suction 
valve on tank TM-1 and the remaining contents of the tank allowed to drain into its containment bund.
About 198bbls of oil was lost from the tank. Most was contained within the drains and the API separator and 
pumped to tank TV-5 or collected by a vacuum truck.
corrective_actions:
Update valve maintenance and inspection protocols. - Review and update valve maintenance protocols. 
Factors to consider may include:
• means to identify rags debris and foreign matter during annual maintenance and repairs
• scheduled stripping and overhauling (or replacement) of critical valves, especially ageing ones
• incorporate borescope or visual inspection steps for valves during maintenance to detect internal contamination, 
material loss and internal condition
• oversight of maintenance contractor

industry: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production
cause: Dropped objects
narrative:
While a Wellhead Engineer was installing a side outlet valve at the wellhead deck, a Floor Man was preparing 
downhole guides on the upper deck level, but one down hole guide clamp, weighing 7 kg, slipped and dropped 
through open hatch and hit the right middle side of the hard hat above the brim and landed in the grating, causing 
the IP to fall on to the grating resulting in bruises to his right forehead and injury to his right knee.
what_went_wrong:
• Inadequate identification of job hazard: The hazards of open hatch, simultaneous operation, drop hazards and its 
control measures are not captured in the Job Safety Analysis.
• Inadequate communication between work groups: Toolbox meeting was not conducted between the service 
company and the Drilling rig crew who are working in the same area.
• Improper handling of materials: The guide and clamps stored close to the open hatch, not considering or 
protecting against the danger of falling objects.
• Inadequate enforcement of PTW: Permit to work was not approved before the start of the work, revalidation of 
permit was not followed when job performer changed.
corrective_actions:
• Review Job Safety Analysis / Risk assessment to include all steps, hazards and controls, with focus on the 
hazards of simultaneous works, drop objects and line of fire and revise accordingly.
• Ensure proper communication is carried out between work groups and with each work team by coordinating 
with different disciplines prior to start.
• Supervisors to ensure that openings are protected with barricades and toe boards to prevent falling objects. 
Also, to conduct walk around to identify loose objects and avoid work near openings.
• Ensure that rig crew are conducting campaigns on “Working at heights & dropped objects” elaborating on risk 
assessment and situational awareness by carrying out weekly site inspections/ verification.
• Conduct Ad-hoc PTW inspection/ verification walk through spotlighting PTW compliance and hazards of 
simultaneous works.
